title: The line of the blind
hook: brahmins who've never seen Brahma are a line of blind men, each holding the one in front

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lohicca and his barber, and your line, share what helps. What good thing did you pass on? Today, two young men arguing on a walk. Day five hundred forty-one.

Two young brahmins, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, are out walking near a village in Kosala, stretching their legs, and arguing. The question is a serious one in their world: which path leads to union with Brahma? Each says it's the path his own teacher teaches. Neither can convince the other. Then they remember that the Buddha is staying nearby, in a mango grove by the river Aciravati. Let's ask him. The thirteenth long discourse is that conversation. Today: the line of the blind.
screen: `TWO STUDENTS, ARGUING ON A WALK.` → `WHICH PATH LEADS TO BRAHMA?` → `LET'S ASK HIM.`

segments.voice: Vasettha puts it generously. All these teachers' paths, he says, maybe they're like the many roads near a village. Different routes, all arriving at the same place. The Buddha doesn't argue with the picture. He asks about the evidence. Vasettha, has any of the brahmins who know the three Vedas seen Brahma face to face? No. Their teachers? No. Their teachers' teachers, back seven generations? No. The ancient sages who composed the verses themselves, did they ever say: we know where Brahma is, we have seen him? No. Then, the Buddha says, it's like a line of blind men, each holding on to the one in front. The first one doesn't see. The one in the middle doesn't see. The last one doesn't see. The Pali is andhaveni: a line, a braid, of the blind. Two things are worth holding carefully here. First, this is a conversation in its own time, between the Buddha and two students, about the specific claims of their teachers. Hindu traditions today understand Brahma, Brahman and the Vedas in many ways, and this text isn't a verdict on them. Second, the image cuts for everyone, including Buddhists. Any teaching passed down hand to hand, by people who trust the person in front, can become a line of the blind. The Buddha's repeated advice is to test. Has anyone in the chain actually seen? Can you see for yourself? And notice, he doesn't stop at criticism. The conversation goes on, and tomorrow, he describes a path the young men can walk and check for themselves.
screen: `MANY ROADS TO ONE VILLAGE?` · `HAS ANYONE SEEN BRAHMA?` · `EACH HOLDING THE ONE IN FRONT` · `THE IMAGE CUTS FOR EVERYONE` · then, large: `THE LINE OF THE BLIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: test one idea you inherited. Choose something you were taught and never checked. About money, about people, about yourself. Picture the line it came down: from whom, and from whom before that. Then ask the Buddha's question: has anyone in this line actually seen it? Have I? You don't have to throw it away. Just hold it as untested for now, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
The line of the blind. A teaching passed hand to hand, each trusting the one in front, with no one who has seen for themselves. Today's word.
screen: `THE LINE OF THE BLIND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the line of the blind. Today, when you repeat something you heard, ask whether anyone along the way actually saw it. Day five hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many schools encourage students to test teachings against their own experience, citing discourses like DN 13 and the Kalama Sutta, while still valuing lineage and the guidance of experienced teachers.

myth: the Buddha begins by mocking the students' teachers
he begins by asking about evidence: has anyone in the line seen Brahma?
the conversation is set near the river Aciravati in Kosala
the Buddha was staying in a mango grove there.
the image only applies to other people's teachings

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. two students ask which path leads to union with Brahma. what do you ask first?
options: has anyone in your teachers' line seen Brahma?
fork.reveal: he traces the line back seven generations and to the ancient sages, and finds no one who claimed to have seen. then he uses the image of a line of the blind.

original.note: Pali andhaveni: a line of the blind, each holding the one in front. veni also means a braid.

trapdoor: what you thought: the line of the blind is an attack on brahmins.
what it means: it asks of any inherited teaching whether anyone along the chain has actually seen.

what a scholar hears: the Tevijja Sutta uses the brahmins' own goal, companionship (sahavyata) with Brahma, and goes on to redefine the path to it through the four immeasurables, a move some scholars read as reinterpretation as much as critique.

notes: DN 13 paraphrased. Confirm the setting (Manasakata in Kosala, the mango grove on the bank of the Aciravati), the two students (Vasettha, pupil of Pokkharasati; Bharadvaja, pupil of Tarukkha), Vasettha's many-roads simile, the seven-generations question, and the Pali andhaveni ('string / braid of the blind').
The framing that this is a conversation within its time and not a verdict on Hindu tradition is deliberate; a Hindu studies reader may wish to check tone.
The trapdoor's scholarly characterization ('reinterpretation as much as critique') is an interpretation (e.g. Gombrich), now attributed to some scholars; confirm.
Do not teach the four immeasurables here; they are tomorrow (day 542).
